To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) addiction is a neurocognitive disorder that is associated with a failure to prioritize long-term consequences of a behavior over short-term consequences; (2) addiction is the product of an interplay between the three neural systems that underlie decision-making and behavior: the reflective system that is associated with the ability to forecast the consequences of a behavior; the impulsive system that is associated to a preference for short-term consequences of behavior; and the insular system that integrates interoceptive states and
the three systems interact to produce the neurobiology of addictive behaviors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural systems that underlie decision-making and the neural basis of addiction.
the neurocognitive approach in understanding the neurobiology underlying addiction and the development of addiction.
understanding the neural mechanisms that underlie the development of drug addiction and relapse.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the three systems interact with each other and with other brain regions to produce the addictive behaviors.
there is a neurocognitive model of addiction that integrates the three systems and that this model is a good starting point to understand the neurobiological basis of addiction.
the three systems model of addiction has provided an important theoretical and empirical advance in understanding the neurobiology and treatment of drug addiction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neural model of addiction can be used to predict addiction vulnerability and treatment outcome.

the neurobiological underpinnings of addictive behavior can be conceptualized as a complex interaction between three neural systems: an amygdala-stria system for automatic, habitual and impulsive behaviors, a prefrontal cortex system that promotes reflective decision-making, and the insula system for integrating interoceptive states into the decision-making process.

we have shown that the three systems interact in a dynamic fashion, with the amygdala-stimulated striatum system driving the decision-making and the insula integrating interoceptive states into the decision-making process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
addiction can be viewed as an imbalance of these three interacting neural systems that lead to poor decision-making.
the three-systems model of addiction can be used to guide the development of new treatment approaches that can be tailored to specific patients.
the neural systems that underlie addiction are the same as those that underlie other behaviors that are not necessarily pathological (e.g. exercise, social behavior, etc.).
